arguments.name: Minimal facts consensus is not merely Christian bias
arguments.conclusion: The scholarly consensus on the minimal facts for the resurrection is not undermined by the fact that many scholars who accept them are Christians, because non-Christian and skeptical scholars also accept them.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: The Jesus Seminar, which dedicated its work to skeptics like David Hume and Thomas Jefferson and praised David Strauss, still admits many of the minimal facts.
P2: James D. G. Dunn, who held a non-orthodox christological view, can be found affirming the six facts repeatedly.
P3: Antony Flew, the world's best-known philosophical atheist at the time, accepted all twelve facts in a debate with Habermas.
P4: If Christian bias were the explanation, the empty tomb would be a minimal fact, but many Christians deny it because they follow the data.

st8.quote: Tony Flew as far as I know when he was an atheist had no problems with the minimal facts. In fact, we started one of the three debates.

arguments.name: Even radical critics like Bultmann support early sources
arguments.conclusion: Even Rudolf Bultmann, a very liberal scholar, affirms key historical data such as a pre-Markan passion narrative and early Jerusalem church sayings, which strengthens the case for the minimal facts.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: Bultmann is listed among critical scholars who accept a pre-Markan passion narrative that may predate AD 37.
P2: Bultmann says the early sayings go back to the very earliest Jerusalem church.
P3: In his 1941 essay, Bultmann states that the earliest disciples preached that Jesus was raised from the dead.
P4: Bultmann is to the left of Bart Ehrman and does not like historical backup for faith, yet he still concedes these points.

arguments.name: Christian scholars debate the evidence, not just assume resurrection

arguments.name: Bultmann himself calls resurrection a myth

arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas

P2: Bultmann does not weigh pros and cons; he already treats it as a myth that did not happen.

arguments.name: Scholarly consensus should target informed scholars who publish
arguments.conclusion: A scholarly consensus argument should focus on scholars who have published in the field of resurrection research because they have informed opinions, not on all PhDs regardless of expertise.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: Scholars like Bethany Hughes have a PhD in history but have never published on resurrection research, so their opinion is uninformed.
P2: We want people who have actually studied the resurrection research and published an opinion.
P3: Habermas defines a critical scholar as one with a terminal degree who has worked in a relevant area such as New Testament, Old Testament, history, philosophy, archaeology, or world religions.
P4: He allows exceptions for people without terminal degrees who know the data, such as G. A. Wells, but generally requires publication or public scholarly engagement.

arguments.name: Habermas is deliberately lenient toward liberal scholars
arguments.conclusion: Habermas's selection criteria are biased in favor of liberal scholars, not conservative ones, because he wants to include critics and give everyone a fair shot.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: He states at the beginning of his book that he is slanted toward liberal scholars.
P2: He includes scholars like Bultmann who are far to the left and not conservative in almost anything.
P3: He makes allowances for people who do not meet his criteria, such as 19th-century German philosophers without terminal degrees, because they are well-known for certain views.
P4: Critics who question his fairness are not reading the data carefully.

st2.quote: I really do think I I'm more lenient with liberals than I am with conservatives because I want to put people in there who don't have all the training, but I want to be honest giving everybody a shot.
